topic: South Indian Dynasties (Rashtrakutas, Cholas, Kakatiyas, Hoysalas, Yadavas)

items.title: The Rashtrakutas (c.753–973 CE)
items.body:
## Rise & Key Rulers

- The Rashtrakutas began as **feudatories of the (Badami) Chalukyas**. **Dantidurga** overthrew Chalukya **Kirtivarman II** (c.753 CE) to found the dynasty; the name means 'he whose elephant is his fortress'.
- **Krishna I** conquered the remaining Chalukya lands and built the **rock-cut Kailasa (Kailashnatha) temple at Ellora** — a monolith carved top-down from a single rock (~200 ft long).
- **Govinda III** was the **greatest military ruler**; his conquests ran from **Kanyakumari to Kanauj** and he defeated the Pratihara **Nagabhatta II**.
- **Amoghavarsha I** (ruled 63 years) shifted the capital to **Manyakheta (Malkhed)**, wrote the **Kavirajamarga** (earliest Kannada poetic work) and was converted to **Jainism by Jinasena**. The Arab **Suleman** ranked him among the world's four greatest kings.
- **Krishna III** was the last powerful ruler; he defeated the Cholas and took Tanjore and Kanchi.

## Culture, Trade & Faith

| Sphere | Highlights |
| --- | --- |
| Literature | Kannada — Pampa (Vikramarjuna Vijaya), Ponna (Santipurana); Sanskrit — Jinasena (Adipurana) |
| Architecture | Dravidian style; Kailasa temple, Ellora |
| Religion | Saivism, Vaishnavism & Jainism coexisted |
| Trade | West-coast/Arab-Deccan overseas trade via port of **Bharuch** |
keyPoints: Dantidurga founded the Rashtrakutas (c.753 CE) by overthrowing Chalukya Kirtivarman II; they were earlier Chalukya feudatories.
Krishna I built the rock-cut monolithic Kailasa temple at Ellora, carved top-down.
Govinda III was the greatest military ruler; conquests from Kanyakumari to Kanauj.
Amoghavarsha I shifted the capital to Manyakheta, wrote Kavirajamarga, and turned to Jainism under Jinasena.
Pampa (greatest Kannada poet) wrote Vikramarjuna Vijaya; Bharuch was the key Rashtrakuta trade port.
items.mnemonic: Rashtrakuta order 'DKG-AK' = Dantidurga → Krishna I → Govinda III → Amoghavarsha I → Krishna III.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Medieval History: Rashtrakutas

items.title: Imperial Cholas — Major Rulers
items.body:
## The Great Chola Emperors

- **Rajaraja I (985–1014)** — originally Arumolivarman; built the **Brihadeeswara temple at Thanjavur** (consecrated 1009–10, vimana ~59.8 m). Conquered the Pandyas, Kerala and northern **Ceylon** (capital Polonnaruva) and annexed the **Maldives**; encouraged the **Chudamani Vihara** at Nagapattinam.
- **Rajendra I (1014–1044)** — assumed the title **Gangaikondachola** after defeating the Pala king **Mahipala** and reaching the Ganga; built the capital **Gangaikondacholapuram**. His **navy invaded the Srivijaya empire** (Sumatra, Java) and he sent **diplomatic missions to China**.
- **Virarajendra** — defeated the Chalukyas and raised a victory pillar on the Tungabhadra.
- **Kulottunga I (1070–1122)** — son of a Vengi prince and a Chola princess; **united the Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi with the Cholas**. Titled **Sungam tavirtta** ('who abolished tolls'); carried out a **land re-survey** and sent 72 merchants to China.

## Naval & Overseas Power

- The Cholas were the dominant **maritime power** of the Bay of Bengal, controlling the sea route to China and Southeast Asian trade.
keyPoints: Rajaraja I built the Brihadeeswara temple at Thanjavur and conquered Ceylon and the Maldives.
Rajendra I took the title Gangaikondachola after defeating Pala king Mahipala and built Gangaikondacholapuram.
Rajendra I's navy invaded Srivijaya (Sumatra/Java); Cholas sent missions to China.
Kulottunga I united the Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi with the Cholas and abolished tolls (Sungam tavirtta).
The Cholas were the dominant maritime power of the Bay of Bengal.
items.mnemonic: 'Raja builds, Rajendra sails' — Rajaraja I = Thanjavur temple; Rajendra I = navy + Gangaikonda.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Medieval History: Imperial Cholas

items.title: Chola Local Self-Government & Village Types
items.body:
## Uttaramerur & the Sabha

- The **Uttaramerur inscriptions of Parantaka I** (c.919/921 CE) record one of the **world's earliest systems of local self-government**.
- The village was divided into **30 wards (kudumbus)**; members were chosen by **lot — kudavolai** ('pot-ticket') — for one year.
- Specialised committees ran affairs: **samvatsaravariyam** (annual), **tottavariyam** (garden), **eri-variyam** (tank), plus pancha-variyam and pon-variyam (gold).
- The **sabha** held proprietary rights over communal land, assessed and collected land revenue, and could tax or remit taxes.

## Three Types of Villages

| Type | Character |
| --- | --- |
| **Ur** | Common village of mixed castes paying land revenue to the king (most frequent) |
| **Brahmadeya** (agrahara) | Granted tax-free to Brahmins; prosperous |
| **Devadana** | Granted to a temple; revenues donated to it |
keyPoints: Uttaramerur inscriptions of Parantaka I record early Chola local self-government.
Village committee members were chosen from 30 wards by the kudavolai (lot/pot-ticket) system for one year.
Key committees: annual (samvatsaravariyam), garden (tottavariyam), tank (eri-variyam).
Ur = ordinary revenue-paying mixed-caste village; Brahmadeya = tax-free Brahmin grant.
Devadana = village granted to a temple, with revenues donated to it.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Medieval History: Imperial Cholas (Administration)

items.title: Chola Art — Temples & Bronzes
items.body:
## Great Living Chola Temples (UNESCO)

- Three 11th–12th-century temples form the UNESCO **'Great Living Chola Temples'**:

| Temple | Place | Builder |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Brihadisvara | **Thanjavur** | Rajaraja I (vimana ~59.8 m) |
| Brihadisvara | **Gangaikondacholapuram** | Rajendra I (completed 1035) |
| Airavatesvara | **Darasuram** | Rajaraja II (ratha-style mandapa) |

## Dravidian Style & Bronze

- Dravidian temples feature a **pyramidal vimana** over the sanctum, pillared **mandapas** and **gopura** gateways.
- The Cholas perfected **lost-wax (cire-perdue) bronze casting**; the **Nataraja** (dancing Shiva) is its finest expression.
- The Thanjavur temple is called **Dakshina Meru** and carries expansive mural paintings.
keyPoints: The three UNESCO Great Living Chola Temples: Thanjavur (Rajaraja I), Gangaikondacholapuram (Rajendra I), Darasuram (Rajaraja II).
Thanjavur Brihadisvara temple is called Dakshina Meru; vimana ~59.8 m.
Dravidian style = pyramidal vimana over the sanctum, pillared mandapas, gopura gateways.
Cholas perfected lost-wax bronze casting; the Nataraja bronze is the finest example.
The Airavatesvara temple at Darasuram has a ratha (chariot) style mandapa.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Medieval History: Imperial Cholas (Art & Architecture); UNESCO

items.title: The Kakatiyas of Warangal (1163–1323)
items.body:
## A Telugu Power

- The Kakatiyas ruled the **Telugu-speaking regions** of present Andhra Pradesh and Telangana, beginning as **Western Chalukya feudatories**. **Prataparudra I** declared independence in **1163 AD**.
- Capitals: **Hanumakonda** first, then permanently **Warangal (Orugallu)** under Ganapati Deva.

## Notable Rulers

| Ruler | Reign | Contribution |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Ganapati Deva** | 1198–1262 | Shifted capital to Warangal; built **Pakhal Lake**; issued **Abhaya Sasanam** for trade at **Motupalli** port; patronised Tikkana |
| **Rudrama Devi** | 1262–1296 | **First woman ruler**; adopted a male title; praised by **Marco Polo** |
| **Prataparudra II** | 1296–1323 | Resisted Khalji/Tughlaq invasions; **Warangal fell to the Tughlaqs in 1323**, ending the dynasty |

## Legacy

- **Tank irrigation** (Pakhal, Ramappa lakes), the **Ramappa (Rudreswara) Temple** — UNESCO World Heritage **2021** — Warangal Fort and the **Thousand Pillar Temple**, and rich **Telugu literature** define the Kakatiya legacy. Their fall opened the Deccan to the Bahmani Sultanate.
keyPoints: Kakatiyas ruled Telugu regions from Warangal; Prataparudra I declared independence from the Chalukyas in 1163.
Ganapati Deva shifted the capital to Warangal, built Pakhal Lake, and issued the Motupalli Abhaya Sasanam.
Rudrama Devi was the first woman ruler, praised by Marco Polo.
Prataparudra II was defeated and Warangal fell to the Tughlaqs in 1323, ending the dynasty.
Ramappa Temple (Palampet) became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2021; tank irrigation was a key legacy.
items.mnemonic: Kakatiya women & waters — Rudrama (queen), Pakhal & Ramappa (tanks), Warangal (fort).
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Medieval History: Regional Kingdoms (Kakatiyas); UNESCO 2021

items.title: Hoysalas & Yadavas of the Deccan
items.body:
## Hoysalas (1050–1355)

- Rose as **Western Chalukya feudatories** in Karnataka. **Vishnuvardhana (1108–1152)** won independence by defeating the **Cholas** and taking **Gangavadi**; converted to **Vaishnavism** under **Ramanujacharya**.
- Capitals: **Belur** and **Halebidu (Dorasamudra)**.
- **Hoysala architecture**: soft **soapstone**, raised **jagati** platform, **star-shaped (stellate)** plan, lathe-turned pillars — e.g. **Chennakesava Temple, Belur** and **Hoysaleswara Temple, Halebidu**.
- Decline: **Veera Ballala III** was killed in the **Battle of Madurai (1343)**; territories merged with the **Vijayanagara Empire**.

## Yadavas / Seunas of Devagiri (1187–1317)

- Ruled the Deccan from **Devagiri (Daulatabad)**. Founder **Bhillama V** declared independence from the Chalukyas (1187).
- **First to adopt Marathi as official language**; developed the mortarless black-stone **Hemadpanti** style (e.g. Gondeshwar Temple, Sinnar). Scholars: **Hemadri**, **Dnyaneshwar** (Dnyaneshwari), **Sarangadeva** (Sangeet Ratnakara).
- Decline: **Malik Kafur** (under Alauddin Khalji) defeated **Ramachandra in 1308**; Delhi fully annexed the kingdom in **1317** (killing Simhana III), beginning Muslim dominance in the Deccan.
keyPoints: Vishnuvardhana founded Hoysala independence by defeating the Cholas; Belur & Halebidu were the capitals.
Hoysala temples used soapstone, a jagati platform and a stellate (star) plan — Chennakesava (Belur), Hoysaleswara (Halebidu).
Veera Ballala III died in the Battle of Madurai (1343); Hoysala lands merged with Vijayanagara.
Yadavas (Seunas) ruled from Devagiri; Bhillama V founded the line and they first made Marathi an official language.
Malik Kafur defeated Ramachandra in 1308; Delhi annexed the Yadava kingdom in 1317.
items.mnemonic: Deccan pair — Hoysala = soapstone stars at Belur/Halebidu; Yadava = Marathi at Devagiri.
items.source: local APPSC GK PDF — Medieval History: Regional Kingdoms (Hoysalas, Yadavas)

items.title: Shivaji & the Maratha State — Ashtapradhan, Revenue, Army
items.body:
## Shivaji (crowned Chhatrapati at Raigad, 1674)

The last great Deccan power, Shivaji built a compact Hindavi Swarajya on efficient administration rather than land grants.

## Ashtapradhan (Council of Eight)

| Minister | Portfolio |
| --- | --- |
| **Peshwa** (Pantpradhan) | Prime minister / general administration |
| **Amatya** (Mazumdar) | Finance & accounts |
| **Sachiv** (Surunavis) | Correspondence / records |
| **Sumant** (Dabir) | Foreign affairs |
| **Senapati** (Sar-i-Naubat) | Commander-in-chief |
| **Nyayadhish** | Chief justice |
| **Panditrao** | Religious & charitable affairs |
| **Waqia-Navis** (Mantri) | Intelligence, posts, household |

- Posts were **non-hereditary** and paid mostly in **cash**.

## Revenue & Military

- **Chauth** = **one-fourth** and **Sardeshmukhi** = an extra **one-tenth**, levied on lands **outside** the Maratha swaraj (**mulk-giri**), not on the core swaraj territory.
- A **cash-paid standing army**; regular cavalry (**bargirs**, state-equipped) vs **silahdars** (own horse & gear); a chain of hill-**forts** and a **navy** (Sindhudurg, Vijaydurg).
keyPoints: Shivaji was crowned Chhatrapati at Raigad in 1674 and founded the Maratha (Hindavi Swarajya) state.
Ashtapradhan = eight ministers; the Peshwa (PM), Amatya (finance), Sumant/Dabir (foreign affairs), Nyayadhish (chief justice).
Chauth (one-fourth) and Sardeshmukhi (extra one-tenth) were levied on external (mulk) lands, not on core swaraj.
Shivaji kept a cash-paid standing army; bargirs used state horses while silahdars brought their own.
He relied on hill-forts and built a navy (Sindhudurg), earning the tag 'father of the Indian navy'.
items.mnemonic: Maratha taxes — 'Chauth = 1/4, Sardeshmukhi = extra 1/10' on mulk (outside) lands.
items.source: NCERT — Medieval India; Britannica — Chauth and Sardeshmukhi (Maratha administration)
